blocks.text: At the beginning of the 20th century, new experiments and theoretical calculations revealed that classical physics, based on Newton's laws, could not explain phenomena involving extremely small particles or very high velocities. This led to the development of relativistic mechanics, which offered a more comprehensive framework than classical mechanics and fundamentally changed our view of the universe. Albert Einstein's Special Theory of Relativity, introduced in 1905, addressed these issues by proposing that the laws of physics are the same for all observers and that the speed of light is constant, regardless of the observer's motion. The theory not only resolved the conflicts between classical mechanics and electromagnetic theory but also revolutionized our understanding of time, space and motion, forming the basis of what is now known as modern physics.

Consider throwing a ball to your right. For someone facing you, this direction appears to be their left; direction is a relative concept. Similarly, the state of rest or motion of an object depends on the observer. For example, the walls of a moving train seem stationary to passengers inside the train but appear to be moving to someone standing on the ground. Thus we cannot definitively say whether an object is absolutely at rest or in motion; all motions are relative to the observer, or to the frame of reference being used.

This becomes evident from the following example. An observer in a closed train compartment uses the compartment as the frame of reference. To find out about the train's motion, the observer drops a ball and measures the horizontal distance travelled by the ball, keeping the vertical distance the same each time; the vertical distance is covered in t seconds in all cases.
Case (a): the train is at rest

The train is stationary. The horizontal velocity of the ball is zero and the horizontal distance travelled is also zero. The observations made by the observer inside the train and by someone outside are identical: the ball falls to a point on the floor directly below the point from which it was dropped (Fig. 11.1a).

blocks.alt: Two pictures of a train at rest on the ground. In each, a person inside the carriage holds out a ball and lets go; the ball's positions form a straight vertical line down to the floor directly below the hand. Left: seen from inside the train. Right: seen by a person standing outside. Below each: v = 0, no horizontal motion; the ball falls straight down.
blocks.caption: Case (a): a ball dropped in a train at rest (original diagram after Fig 11.1a).

blocks.text: Case (b): the train moves with uniform velocity v0

The train moves with a uniform velocity v0. When released, the ball has an initial horizontal velocity v0 and behaves like a projectile, travelling a horizontal distance v0 t in the time t it takes to reach the floor. Since the train and the observer inside it move with the same velocity v0, they travel the same horizontal distance v0 t in the same time. Therefore the observer inside sees the ball fall to a point directly below where it was dropped, while an observer outside sees the ball follow a projectile path (Fig. 11.1b).

blocks.alt: Left, seen from inside: a train moving to the right at v0; a person inside drops a ball, and its positions form a straight vertical line down to the floor below the hand. Right, seen from the ground: the train is shown where it was when the ball was let go (dashed) and where it is when the ball lands (solid), v0 t further on; the ball's positions form a curved projectile path from the hand in the first position to the floor below the hand in the second.
blocks.caption: Case (b): a ball dropped in a train moving with uniform velocity v0 (original diagram after Fig 11.1b).

blocks.text: Thus, observers in different frames of reference, moving with uniform velocity relative to each other, will perceive motion differently.
